learning.javascript:
Adding to the end of a string

result += x is short for result = result + x: it builds a new string from result and x, and makes result name the new one. The old string isn't changed (strings can't be), but result no longer refers to it. It's how a string is built up in steps:

let result = "h";
result += "I";            // result is now "hI"
result += "!";            // "hI!"

Declare it with let: += gives the variable a new value, and a const can't be given one (TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.).

See Addition assignment (+=) on MDN.

learning.cpp:
Adding to the end of a string

result += x adds x to the end of result itself: a std::string can be changed, so, unlike in the other languages, no new string is made. It's how a string is built up in steps:

string result = "h";
result += "I";            // result is now "hI"
result += "!";            // "hI!"

See operator+= on cppreference.

Adding to the end of a string

result += x is short for result = result + x: it builds a new String from result and x, and makes result name the new one. The old String isn't changed (Strings can't be), but result no longer refers to it. It's how a String is built up in steps:

String result = "h";
result += "I";                  // result is now "hI"
result += "!";                  // "hI!"

learning.d:
Adding to the end of a string

result ~= x appends x to the end of result. The characters already in result aren't changed (they can't be); x's are added after them. It's how a string is built up in steps:

string result = "h";
result ~= "I";            // result is now "hI"
result ~= "!";            // "hI!"

See Arrays in the D language specification: a string is an array.
